results.result: After exposure to a motion sequence, presenting only the first or last stimulus (cue) elicited elevated neural responses during periods corresponding to the second and third stimuli in the full sequence, but not the fourth stimulus. These cue-triggered elevated responses were observed in both start-only and end-only conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C27 provide converging statistical evidence from ERF analyses showing significant peaks during the second and third RDK intervals (p<10^-3 to 10^-5) but not the fourth interval (p>0.2) in both start-only and end-only conditions. The results are well-documented with appropriate statistical tests and replicate prior findings with more complex stimuli.

results.result: Motion direction information could be decoded during full sequence trials and for the cue in start/end-only trials, but subsequent motion direction information was absent at the group level during the post-cue blank period. The cue-triggered elevated responses were not consistently feature-specific across participants and trials.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C34 demonstrate through time-resolved decoding analyses that while the cue could be reliably decoded (surpassing permutation thresholds), subsequent motion directions during the blank period showed no consistent feature-specific patterns at the group level. This is a key negative finding that is appropriately supported by the decoding analyses and permutation testing.

results.result: Backward replay of the exposed motion sequence was detected during the post-cue blank period in both start-only and end-only conditions, with peak transition lags at 28-40 ms and 28-36 ms respectively. The replay was approximately 10 times faster than the original sequence and occurred predominantly in the middle-to-late stages of the blank period. Control analyses confirmed only backward replay was detected among all 24 possible sequences.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C41 provide robust evidence for backward replay using TDLM analysis with appropriate statistical thresholds (p<0.042, FWE corrected). The temporal specificity (C39-C40), speed compression (C38), and control analyses (C41) strengthen the finding. Statistical tests are appropriate and the effect is replicated across conditions.

results.result: No evidence of forward or backward replay was found when the second or third stimulus of the sequence was presented as a cue (Experiment 2).
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C43 demonstrate through TDLM analysis that replay is cue-dependent, occurring only when sequence boundaries (first or last stimuli) are presented. The negative finding is appropriately reported with effect sizes (β values) that did not reach significance, providing important constraints on the phenomenon.

results.result: Brief exposure to the sequence (Experiment 3, without dedicated exposure phase) induced a trend for backward replay in the start-only condition (non-significant) and significant backward replay in the end-only condition at 20-40 ms transition lags.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C45 show mixed results: the start-only condition showed only a numerical trend (non-significant), while the end-only condition just reached significance (p<0.042). The inconsistency between conditions and marginal significance in one condition makes it uncertain whether brief exposure reliably induces replay. Additional replication would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: Replay events were associated with transient ripple power increase (120-180 Hz) localized to bilateral visual cortex. MTL activation preceded visual cortex activation by 30 ms, with peak MTL activation occurring before peak visual cortex activation at replay onset.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C50 provide converging evidence from time-frequency analysis, source localization, and temporal dynamics showing ripple power increases in visual cortex and earlier MTL activation. The 30 ms temporal precedence is statistically significant (p<0.05, corrected) and the spatial localization is appropriate. However, MEG source localization has inherent spatial resolution limitations that should be acknowledged.

results.result: Prediction-related elevated responses in dynamic temporal contexts are not feature-specific, potentially facilitating general processing of any upcoming stimuli rather than stimuli with specific features.
results.evaluation: Claim C56 is directly supported by the experimental findings (C33-C34) showing absence of feature-specific decoding during elevated responses. However, C57's functional interpretation is speculative. The contrast with prior work on static contexts is appropriate, but the proposed function requires direct behavioral or additional neural evidence.

results.result: Brief exposure to a visual sequence is sufficient to induce replay, which may play a critical role in memorizing the visual sequence.
results.evaluation: Claim C58 is partially supported by Experiment 3 results (C44-C45), but the evidence is mixed with only one condition reaching significance. Claim C59 about the functional role in memory is entirely speculative without behavioral memory measures or direct tests of the relationship between replay and memory performance.

results.result: Non-feature-specific elevated responses could be induced by rhythmic entrainment, where rhythmic presentation of the motion sequence entrains oscillatory activity leading to periodic activation of sensory cortices, facilitating general neural processing independent of specific stimulus features.
results.evaluation: Claims C60, C63-C64 are speculative mechanistic interpretations not directly tested in the study. While C61-C62 cite relevant prior work on rhythmic entrainment, the current study did not measure entrainment, oscillatory phase relationships, or test predictions of the entrainment hypothesis. This remains a plausible but untested explanation.

results.result: Feature-specific replay operates through intrinsic neural processes not time-locked to stimulus onset, manifesting spontaneously and potentially facilitating integration of fragmented experiences into coherent representations for visual sequence learning and memory.
results.evaluation: Claim C66 is supported by the data showing non-time-locked replay (C36-C37, C39-C40). However, claims C65 and C67 about intrinsic mechanisms and functional roles are speculative interpretations without direct mechanistic tests or behavioral validation linking replay to learning outcomes.

results.result: Elevated responses may originate in visual cortex through local synaptic mechanisms without hippocampal involvement, while replay events are likely initiated by the hippocampus and involve active communication between hippocampus and visual cortex, with the hippocampus encoding stimulus relationships and visual cortex serving as a platform for replay manifestation.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C69 cite relevant prior work but the current study did not directly test the origin of elevated responses. Claims C70-C72 are speculative interpretations of the MTL-visual cortex temporal relationship (C49-C50). While the temporal precedence is consistent with hippocampal initiation, alternative explanations (e.g., common input, indirect pathways) are not ruled out. Claim C73 cites supporting theory but requires direct causal manipulation.

results.result: Visual sequence exposure induces twofold brain plasticity: time-locked, non-feature-specific elevated responses and non-time-locked, feature-specific backward replay that occurs in a time-compressed manner and can be triggered only by the first or last stimulus of the sequence.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C53 and C93 accurately summarize the main experimental findings supported by multiple results (elevated responses: C22-C27; lack of feature-specificity: C33-C34; backward replay: C36-C37; time compression: C38; cue-dependence: C42-C43, C53). This represents a well-supported synthesis of the core findings.

results.result: Non-feature-specific elevated responses may enhance general processing of upcoming visual stimuli, whereas feature-specific backward replay may subserve visual sequence learning and memory.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C95 propose functional interpretations of the two types of plasticity but are speculative without direct behavioral evidence. The study did not measure learning outcomes, memory performance, or processing efficiency to test these proposed functions. These remain plausible hypotheses requiring future validation.

results.result: Motion direction decoding from MEG signals peaked at 411-464 ms after stimulus onset with 53-58% accuracy, showing no significant differences among the four motion directions in latency or accuracy. The trained classifiers for different motion directions showed no spatial correlation (r<0.12).
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C30 report appropriate validation of the decoding approach with clear statistical tests (F-tests, p-values) and effect sizes. Claim C35 demonstrates classifier independence, which is important for subsequent TDLM analyses. The decoding accuracies are modest but significantly above chance and appropriate for MEG data.

results.result: A total of 59 participants were recruited across three experiments, with appropriate exclusion criteria applied (excessive head motion >20mm, chance-level performance). Sample sizes were comparable to previous studies in the field.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C99 provide transparent reporting of sample sizes, exclusion criteria, and justification. The exclusion criteria are reasonable and clearly stated. While no formal power analysis was conducted (C99), the sample sizes (n=18-21 per experiment after exclusions) are adequate for within-subject MEG designs and comparable to cited prior work.

results.result: Prior work establishes that cortical plasticity can be induced by both active training and passive exposure, with cue-triggered reactivation being prediction-related and expectation sharpening neural tuning in static contexts.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C11 appropriately cite and summarize relevant prior literature establishing the background for the current study. These claims are well-supported by the cited references and provide appropriate context for the research questions.

results.result: Prior work demonstrates that replay is associated with memory consolidation and learning following temporal sequence training, involving sequential reactivation of neural patterns in temporally compressed forward or backward directions, often coinciding with hippocampal sharp-wave ripples.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C20 accurately summarize the replay literature with appropriate citations. This background is essential for contextualizing the current findings and is well-supported by the cited references.

results.result: Prior work supports that hippocampal-neocortical communication is critical for replay events, with the hippocampus encoding stimulus relationships and replay offering a mechanism for transferring experience to cortex. Visual sequence exposure leads to visual sequence learning, and hippocampal damage impairs both relationship encoding and visual sequence plasticity.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C82 cite relevant prior work supporting the theoretical framework for interpreting the current findings. The citations are appropriate and the synthesis provides a coherent theoretical context for the hippocampal-cortical interaction hypothesis.

results.result: Prior work shows that replay can occur in forward or backward directions in both rodents and humans, with proposed functional differences (forward for planning, backward for experience) though the exact function remains unclear. Replay is sensitive to sequence boundaries, with start and end points serving as anchors for place cell firing and potentially triggering replay onset.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C92 appropriately review the literature on replay directionality and boundary sensitivity, providing important context for interpreting the backward replay and cue-dependence findings. The acknowledgment of uncertainty about functional roles (C88) is appropriate given the mixed evidence in the literature.

results.result: After exposure to motion sequences, presenting only the first or last stimulus (start-only or end-only trials) elicited time-locked elevated neural responses during periods corresponding to the missing stimuli, though no peak was observed for the final interval. These cue-triggered elevated responses resembled those from full sequence trials.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirmed this finding, with one reviewer stating 'Identifying the two types of activation after exposure to a sequence of motion directions is very interesting' and another noting that 'showing either the starting movement direction, or ending movement direction causes a coarse-grained brain response that is similar to that elicited by the complete sequence.' The experimental design and analyses were described as 'solid.'

results.result: While motion direction information could be decoded in full sequence trials and for the cue stimulus in start/end-only trials, subsequent motion direction information was absent at the group level during the post-cue blank period. This indicates the cue-triggered elevated response was not consistently feature-specific across participants and trials.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this finding, with one explicitly noting 'they show by decoding the sensor responses that this brain activity actually does not carry information about the actual sequence and the motion directions, at least not on the time scale of the initial sequence.' The editor described the evidence as 'convincing evidence for both feature-specific and non-specific sequence representations.'

results.result: Using temporally delayed linear modeling (TDLM), backward replay of the exposed motion sequence was detected during the post-cue blank period in both start-only and end-only conditions, with peak transition lags at 28-40 ms. The replayed sequence was approximately 10 times faster than the evoked activity sequence, and only backward replay was detected when examining all potential sequences.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirmed this finding as a key contribution. One reviewer stated 'They also show a reverse reply on a highly-compressed time scale, which is elicited during the period of elevated activity.' The editor described this as 'convincing evidence' and noted that 'finding such replays in humans is novel.' The statistical methodology was deemed 'valid' though complex.

results.result: In Experiment 2, when the second or third stimulus (rather than first or last) was presented as a cue, no evidence of forward or backward replay was found in either condition.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this control experiment finding without challenge. One reviewer noted that replay was 'activated by the first and last elements of the sequence, but not others,' implicitly affirming the Experiment 2 results. This finding supports the boundary-sensitivity interpretation of replay.

results.result: In Experiment 3 with brief exposure (no pre-exposure phase), a numerical trend of backward replay was found in the start-only condition (not reaching significance), while the end-only condition just reached significance. This suggests even brief exposure can induce a trend for backward replay.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this finding as part of the overall pattern of results. One reviewer noted the findings are 'interesting and novel,' and the experimental procedures were described as 'solid.' The claim about brief exposure inducing replay trends aligns with the reviewers' acceptance of the broader replay findings.

results.result: Replay events were associated with transient ripple power increases at 120-180 Hz localized to bilateral visual cortex. Critically, the right MTL (including hippocampus and amygdala) showed power increases 30 ms prior to visual cortex activation, suggesting information flow from MTL to visual cortex.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirmed this finding. One reviewer stated 'The finding that activity in the medial temporal lobe (MTL) preceded that in the visual cortex suggests that the visual cortex may serve as a platform for the manifestation of replay events.' Another noted 'these replays seem to occur during periods of cortical ripples, similar to what is found in animal studies.' The sophisticated MEG analyses were deemed convincing.

results.result: Visual sequence exposure induces twofold brain plasticity: time-locked, non-feature-specific elevated responses and non-time-locked, feature-specific backward replay that occurs in a time-compressed manner and can only be triggered by the first or last stimulus of the sequence.
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly supported this overarching finding. The editor described it as a 'valuable study' with 'convincing evidence for both feature-specific and non-specific sequence representations.' One reviewer stated 'Identifying the two types of activation after exposure to a sequence of motion directions is very interesting' and that 'The findings are interesting and novel.' The distinction between the two types of plasticity was central to reviewers' positive assessment.

results.result: Unlike expectation-based responses in static contexts which are feature-specific, prediction-related elevated responses in dynamic temporal contexts are not feature-specific, potentially facilitating general processing of any upcoming stimuli rather than stimuli with specific features.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this interpretation as part of the study's contribution. One reviewer noted the study 'shows that this brain activity actually does not carry information about the actual sequence and the motion directions,' supporting the non-feature-specific nature. The editor's description of 'non-specific sequence representations' as a key finding affirms this claim.

results.result: Contrary to prevailing notions that replay requires lengthy training, even brief exposure to a visual sequence is sufficient to induce replay, which may play a critical role in memorizing the visual sequence.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this finding as novel and important. One reviewer stated the findings are 'interesting and novel,' and the editor noted that 'finding such replays in humans is novel.' The experimental evidence from Experiment 3 showing replay trends with brief exposure supports this claim, and reviewers raised no objections to this interpretation.

results.result: The non-feature-specific elevated responses could be induced by rhythmic entrainment, where rhythmic presentation of the motion sequence entrains oscillatory activity leading to periodic activation of sensory cortices, serving as a mechanism for general facilitation of neural processing independent of specific stimulus features.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge this mechanistic interpretation. While speculative, it is presented as a plausible explanation supported by prior literature. The reviewers' acceptance of the non-feature-specific nature of elevated responses and their description of the experimental design and analyses as 'solid' implicitly supports this mechanistic account.

results.result: Feature-specific replay operates through a different mechanism driven by intrinsic neural processes rather than direct external stimuli, manifesting spontaneously rather than time-locked to stimulus onset, and may facilitate integration of fragmented experiences into coherent representations for visual sequence learning and memory.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this interpretation. One reviewer initially questioned 'why the second type of activation was suggested to occur spontaneously' but noted 'this concern has been satisfactorily addressed in the revision,' indicating the authors successfully clarified the spontaneous, non-time-locked nature of replay. The mechanistic distinction between the two types of plasticity was central to reviewers' positive evaluation.

results.result: Replay events are likely initiated by the hippocampus and involve active communication between the hippocampus and visual cortex, with the hippocampus encoding relationships among stimuli while visual cortex acts as a platform for manifestation of replay events.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirmed this interpretation. One reviewer stated 'The finding that activity in the medial temporal lobe (MTL) preceded that in the visual cortex suggests that the visual cortex may serve as a platform for the manifestation of replay events, which potentially enhance visual sequence learning.' The temporal precedence finding (C48-C50) provides empirical support for this mechanistic claim.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on C22-C27. Both evaluations find the ERF evidence for elevated responses during second and third RDK intervals strongly supported. OpenEval emphasizes statistical rigor (p-values, replication), while peer reviewers highlight the novelty and solid experimental design.

Perfect agreement on C31-C34. Both evaluations support the finding that elevated responses lack feature-specific information. OpenEval characterizes this as an 'appropriate negative finding,' while peer reviewers describe it as 'convincing evidence' for non-specific representations.

Perfect agreement on C36-C41. Both evaluations strongly support the backward replay findings. OpenEval emphasizes statistical robustness and temporal specificity, while peer reviewers highlight the novelty of finding replay in humans and describe the methodology as 'valid' though complex.

Perfect agreement on C42-C43. Both evaluations support the cue-dependence finding from Experiment 2. OpenEval notes the appropriate reporting of negative findings, while peer reviewers accept this as supporting boundary-sensitivity interpretation without challenge.

Disagreement on C44-C45, C54. OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to mixed results (only end-only condition significant, start-only showing only numerical trend) and calls for replication. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, accepting the findings as 'interesting and novel' without expressing concerns about the marginal significance.

Agreement on C46-C50, C55 with minor differences. Both support the ripple-MTL-visual cortex findings. OpenEval acknowledges MEG spatial resolution limitations, while peer reviewers emphasize the sophisticated analyses and similarity to animal studies without noting methodological caveats.

Partial disagreement on C56-C57. Both agree C56 is supported by data (C33-C34). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED but explicitly flags C57's functional interpretation as speculative requiring additional evidence. Peer reviewers rate SUPPORTED without distinguishing between empirical finding and functional speculation.

Disagreement on C58-C59. OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN, noting C58 has mixed evidence (only one condition significant) and C59 is entirely speculative without behavioral measures. Peer reviewers rate SUPPORTED, accepting the findings as 'novel' without expressing concerns about the speculative nature or mixed evidence.

Disagreement on C60-C64. OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN, noting these are speculative mechanistic interpretations not directly tested (no entrainment measurements or phase relationships). Peer reviewers rate SUPPORTED, accepting the mechanistic account as plausible without challenging the lack of direct evidence.

Disagreement on C65-C67. OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN, accepting C66 as data-supported but flagging C65 and C67 as speculative without mechanistic tests or behavioral validation. Peer reviewers rate SUPPORTED, noting initial concerns were 'satisfactorily addressed in revision' regarding spontaneous nature.

Perfect agreement on C51-C53, C93. Both evaluations strongly support this synthesis of main findings. OpenEval describes it as 'well-supported synthesis of core findings,' while peer reviewers characterize it as 'valuable study' with 'convincing evidence' for both types of plasticity.

Partial overlap on C70-C73. OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN for C68-C73, noting temporal precedence is consistent with hippocampal initiation but alternative explanations not ruled out. Peer reviewers rate SUPPORTED for C70-C73 specifically, explicitly affirming the MTL-to-visual-cortex interpretation based on temporal precedence data.

OpenEval rates C94-C95 as UNCERTAIN, noting functional interpretations are speculative without behavioral evidence linking to learning outcomes or processing efficiency. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific claims.

OpenEval rates C28-C30, C35 as SUPPORTED, affirming the decoding validation methodology with appropriate statistical tests and classifier independence. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing these methodological validation claims.

OpenEval rates C96-C99 as SUPPORTED, noting transparent reporting of sample sizes and reasonable exclusion criteria, though no formal power analysis conducted. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing these methodological reporting claims.

OpenEval rates C1-C11 as SUPPORTED, affirming the background literature on elevated responses and temporal context is appropriately cited and summarized. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these background claims.

OpenEval rates C12-C20 as SUPPORTED, affirming the replay literature background is accurately summarized with appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these background claims.

OpenEval rates C74-C82 as SUPPORTED, affirming the theoretical framework citations for hippocampal-cortical interactions are appropriate and provide coherent context. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these theoretical background claims.

OpenEval rates C83-C92 as SUPPORTED, affirming the literature review on replay directionality and boundary sensitivity appropriately contextualizes findings and acknowledges uncertainty about functional roles. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these background claims.
